title: Types of Urban Data and Databases
topicSummary: Types of data and data format, Types of databases, Relational databases, Database normalization, NoSQL.

content.text: Urban data is generated continuously from multiple sources within a city ecosystem.

📖 Reading Note: A helpful analogy — structured data is like data in an Excel sheet (neat rows and columns), semi-structured is like a WhatsApp message with hashtags (partially organized), and unstructured is like a CCTV recording (no labeling at all, raw video). In urban analytics, unstructured data (like images from traffic cameras) is processed using CNNs (Convolutional Neural Networks) to extract structured information like vehicle counts or speed.

📖 Reading Note: Chennai's flood monitoring system (2015 flood aftermath) is a real example of multi-source data integration. The system now combines: (1) sensor data from rain gauges, (2) administrative data from CMDA drainage maps, (3) crowdsourced data from Aapathukal emergency app (citizen flood reports), and (4) geospatial satellite imagery. By fusing all four source types, the city generates flood risk heatmaps 6 hours in advance.
Data format defines how data is stored and exchanged.
Key Insight: Format selection affects: Storage efficiency, Processing speed, Interoperability.

📖 Reading Note: GeoJSON is worth understanding well — it is the standard format for mapping web applications. A GeoJSON file looks like this: {"type": "Feature", "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [77.59, 12.97]}, "properties": {"name": "Lalbagh", "type": "park"}}. You can drop any GeoJSON file into geojson.io to visualize it instantly on a map — a great tool for urban data exploration. OpenStreetMap data is also exported in GeoJSON or XML for city-level analysis.
Databases are systems used to store, manage, and retrieve data efficiently.

📖 Reading Note: In practice, smart city platforms use a mix of all four database types. Example — Pune Smart City Command Centre uses: (1) PostgreSQL (relational) for citizen records, (2) MongoDB (NoSQL) for IoT device event logs, (3) PostGIS (spatial) for GIS-based zoning data, and (4) AWS RDS (cloud) for scalable storage. Understanding when to use each is a core skill in Urban Informatics.
Definition: A relational database organizes data into tables (relations) with rows and columns.

📖 Reading Note: The BRTS (Bus Rapid Transit System) database in Ahmedabad is built on PostgreSQL (relational). Each bus trip is a row, with columns for route_id, departure_time, passenger_count, fuel_used. By linking the trips table (via foreign key route_id) to a routes table, planners quickly query 'which route has the highest passenger load on Mondays between 8am-10am?' — and allocate extra buses accordingly. This is RDBMS solving real urban problems.
Definition: Normalization is the process of organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity.
Student "A" repeated across ML and DB courses in a single row.
👉 Outcome: Cleaner database, faster queries, reduced anomalies.

📖 Reading Note: A common urban database mistake (before normalization): An electricity board stores customer name, address, meter_id, and bill_amount all in one table. When the customer moves, their name and address appear in 1,000 rows — updating all 1,000 is error-prone. After normalization: a Customers table (customer_id, name, address) and a Bills table (bill_id, customer_id, amount, date) linked by customer_id. Now one address change updates exactly one row. This is why 3NF is a standard in government data systems.
Definition: NoSQL databases store data in non-tabular formats, allowing flexibility.

📖 Reading Note: Graph databases (like Neo4j) are particularly powerful for urban network analysis. Example: Model a city's metro network as a graph — each station is a 'node' and each track section is an 'edge' with weight = travel time. You can then run shortest-path algorithms (like Dijkstra's) directly inside the database query to find the fastest route from Whitefield to Majestic in Bengaluru metro. This is exactly how navigation apps like Google Maps work internally — graph databases powering spatial queries.

items: Traffic Systems: SQL → structured traffic logs, NoSQL → real-time sensor data
Smart Cities: Spatial DB → maps and GIS, Cloud DB → scalable storage
Urban Analytics: JSON APIs → live city data

content.text: How Week 2 Concepts Connect Across the Course:

rows: CNNs are specifically designed to process unstructured image data (traffic cameras, satellite imagery) which cannot go into SQL tables
APIs return JSON; GIS platforms exchange GeoJSON — understanding formats is essential before accessing data in Week 3
Week 3 builds directly on Week 2 — SQL syntax is learned in Week 3, but the table/key concepts originate here
Normalization prevents data anomalies at the storage level; data cleaning in Week 5 fixes anomalies at the analysis level — two layers of the same problem
IoT devices generate real-time, variable-schema data that NoSQL (MongoDB, Cassandra) handles efficiently — Week 10's cloud integration builds on this
PostGIS (Week 12) is a specific spatial database — the concept introduced here is the foundation for Week 12's geospatial SQL queries

content.text: 🔗 Big Picture: Week 2 is the 'data architecture' layer. Every tool used later — SQL in Week 3, Pandas in Week 5, cloud storage in Week 10, PostGIS in Week 12 — requires knowing what kind of database stores what kind of data. When you encounter a new urban dataset, Week 2 is the mental checklist: What structure? What format? What database type fits best?
